fields.claim_quote: The resulting graph has $n$ vertices. Apply the inductive hypothesis - this graph has at least $n - 1$ edges.
fields.explanation: The graph with edges 01,02,14,15,23,26,36,45 is connected and has degrees [2,3,3,2,2,2,2]. Thus deleting vertex 0 is allowed by the instruction to remove a minimum-degree vertex. The remaining graph consists of the disjoint triangles {1,4,5} and {2,3,6}, so the connected-graph induction hypothesis does not apply. The selected theorem certifies this example only. It does not establish an enumeration count, minimality across all smaller graphs, or a claim about choosing a unique minimum-degree vertex. The final connected-graph edge bound is not refuted.
fields.flaw: Step 2 implicitly claims that after removing a lowest-degree vertex (step 1) from a connected graph on n+1 vertices, the inductive hypothesis P(n) -- which is stated only for CONNECTED graphs -- can be applied to the resulting n-vertex graph. This requires the resulting graph to be connected, which is false in general: a lowest-degree vertex can be a cut vertex, so the resulting graph may be disconnected and the precondition of the inductive hypothesis fails.
fields.problem: Inductively the number of edges for a connected graph
fields.source_context:
0001 | Claim: Every connected graph with $n$ vertices has at least $n - 1$ edges.
0002 | 
0003 | Proof by induction:
0004 | 
0005 | $P(n)$ = "Every connected graph with $n$ vertices has at least $n - 1$ edges." $\forall n \ge 1$
0006 | 
0007 | Base case: A graph with $1$ vertex has $0$ edges.
0008 | 
0009 | Inductive step:
0010 | 
0011 | 1. Remove a vertex with the lowest degree and all its edges from the connected graph with $n + 1$ vertices.
0012 | 
0013 | 2. The resulting graph has $n$ vertices. Apply the inductive hypothesis - this graph has at least $n - 1$ edges.
0014 | 
0015 | 3. When you add the removed vertex back, it must connect to at least $1$ vertex in order for the overall graph to be connected.
0016 | 
0017 | 4. The graph now contains at least $n - 1 + 1$ or $n$ edges
0018 | 
0019 | I'm new to graph theory, so I'm wondering if I completed this induction proof with the right steps. Any other methods or additions to this proof would also be appreciated. Thanks!
fields.witness: Take the graph on{0,...,6} with edges01,02,14,15,23,26,36,45. It is connected and has degrees[2,3,3,2,2,2,2], so0 is a permitted minimum-degree vertex. Deleting0 leaves disjoint triangles{1,4,5} and{2,3,6}. The induction hypothesis only covers connected graphs and cannot be applied to that result. This is the seven-vertex counterexample certified by the selected declaration; no exact enumeration count or global minimality claim is needed.
